claims.text: An ML model integrating DFT-derived phonon descriptors will identify low-lattice-thermal-conductivity HEAs more accurately than empirical correlations or simplified scattering models.
Phonon dispersion curves, mode-localization metrics, and scattering rates can serve as physics-based descriptors for the proposed ML model.
Chemical disorder in HEAs produces force-constant fluctuations that increase phonon scattering.
Chemical disorder in HEAs causes localization of vibrational modes.
Lattice distortion can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, resulting in low lattice thermal conductivity.
DFT-derived descriptors can quantify disorder-induced localization and scattering sufficiently for an ML model to learn the mechanism governing lattice thermal conductivity.
A lattice thermal conductivity below 0.5 W/mK at 300 K is a critical threshold for thermal-insulation applications.
The approach is intended for disordered, single-phase, multi-principal-element HEAs at room to moderately high temperatures.
The intended evaluation-temperature range is approximately 300–700 K.
The approach applies only within composition and disorder regimes represented in the training data and maintaining a stable, disordered single phase.
HEAs selected by the physics-informed model will experimentally exhibit lattice thermal conductivity below 0.5 W/mK at 300 K.
The physics-informed model will have a lower prediction error or a higher reliable-identification rate than conventional models.
Conventional empirical or simplified phonon-scattering models typically have only moderate prediction success and larger deviations from measured thermal conductivities.
Model accuracy may diminish for extreme compositions, ordered or multiphase structures, and temperatures or disorder levels outside the training domain.
Previous studies of HEAs and related thermoelectric materials support an association between disorder or lattice distortion, enhanced phonon scattering, and low lattice thermal conductivity.
The benchmark will compare HEAs selected by the integrated model with control samples selected using conventional predictive methods.
Phase and microstructure characterization will be used to verify that benchmark samples remain within the model's applicability regime.
The hypothesis is falsified if model-selected HEAs fail to remain below 0.5 W/mK and the model shows no statistically significant improvement over conventional methods.
